topic.subject: science
topic.title: Heat and temperature
topic.scope: heat vs temperature, thermometers, conduction, convection, radiation, sea and land breeze, dark vs light clothes

misconceptions.statement: Heat and temperature are the same thing.
misconceptions.why: In everyday language, people use the words interchangeably when describing weather or cooking.
misconceptions.fix: Temperature measures how hot or cold an object is, while heat is the total energy transferred between objects due to a temperature difference.

probe.question: If you add more hot water to a cup, does the heat increase or the temperature?
probe.wrong_answer: The heat increases because the water is hot.

misconceptions.why: Students often perceive heat as a substance or fluid that resides within an object rather than energy in transit.
misconceptions.fix: Heat is energy that is moving from a warmer object to a cooler one; objects contain internal energy, not 'heat'.

probe.question: Where does the heat go when you take a hot spoon out of tea?
probe.wrong_answer: The heat stays inside the spoon for a while.

misconceptions.statement: Cold moves from the ice to the hand.
misconceptions.why: Language like 'the cold is coming in' suggests cold is an active agent that travels, similar to heat.
misconceptions.fix: Cold is simply the absence of heat; heat always moves from the warmer object to the cooler one.

probe.question: Why does your hand feel cold when holding an ice cube?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the cold from the ice moves into my hand.

misconceptions.statement: Metals are naturally warm to the touch.
misconceptions.why: Students touch a metal object and feel it is colder than wood, leading them to think metal has a 'cold' property.
misconceptions.fix: Metal is a good conductor, so it draws heat away from your hand faster than wood, making it feel colder.

probe.question: Why does a metal spoon feel colder than a plastic spoon in the same room?
probe.wrong_answer: Because metal is a cold material and plastic is a warm material.

misconceptions.why: Students observe smoke or hot air rising and overgeneralize this to all heat transfer.
misconceptions.fix: Heat can travel in any direction; convection currents occur in fluids because hot fluid becomes less dense and rises, but radiation travels in all directions.

probe.question: If you hold your hand to the side of a candle flame, why do you feel heat?
probe.wrong_answer: I shouldn't feel heat because heat only goes up.

misconceptions.statement: Dark clothes absorb heat from the sun, but light clothes do not.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse 'absorbing heat' with 'creating heat', thinking light clothes have a property that repels heat.
misconceptions.fix: All objects absorb some radiation, but dark colors are better absorbers and emitters of heat than light colors.

probe.question: Do light-colored clothes absorb any heat from the sun?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they reflect all the heat and don't absorb any.
